blocks.text: A stainless steel kitchen sink bowl is made by pressing a flat sheet into a die in one stroke. If the press is set up wrongly, the rim of the bowl wrinkles like a frilly collar or the bottom tears out cleanly. Whether you get a good bowl depends on how far the metal is asked to flow inward and how firmly the edge of the sheet is held.

blocks.markdown: In **deep drawing** a flat sheet blank of diameter $D$ and thickness $t$ is held over a die opening by a blank holder, and a punch of diameter $d$ pushes the centre of the blank into the die. The outer part of the blank, the **flange**, is pulled radially inward over the die radius and becomes the wall of the cup. Because a ring of metal must squeeze into a smaller circumference, the flange is in radial tension and circumferential compression, while the cup wall at the punch corner carries the whole drawing load in tension.

blocks.title: Draw ratio and limiting drawing ratio
blocks.text: The draw ratio is $D/d$, the blank diameter divided by the punch (cup) diameter. The limiting drawing ratio (LDR) is the largest $D/d$ that can be drawn in one operation without tearing. For many sheet metals the LDR is about 1.8 to 2.0 on a first draw; this is a typical range, and the actual value depends on material, lubrication and tooling radii.

blocks.markdown: The blank size follows from conservation of material. Sheet thickness changes little in drawing, so we equate the surface area of the finished cup to the area of the blank. For a flat-bottomed cylindrical cup of inside diameter $d$ and height $h$, ignoring corner radii and wall thinning, the cup area is the base $\pi d^2/4$ plus the wall $\pi d h$. Setting that equal to $\pi D^2/4$ gives the formula below.

blocks.title: Blank diameter and draw ratio
blocks.prompt: A cylindrical cup of inside diameter $d=60$ mm and height $h=40$ mm is to be drawn in one operation from sheet. Find the blank diameter, the draw ratio and check it against an LDR of 2.0.

steps.latex: Since 1.91 is below 2.0, a single draw is feasible; a ratio close to the limit would call for good lubrication and generous die radius.

blocks.answer: The blank diameter is about 115 mm and the draw ratio is 1.91, within the typical LDR, so one draw should work.

blocks.markdown: Why is there a limit? The punch force is transmitted to the flange through the wall of the cup at the punch corner. If the force needed to draw the flange inward exceeds the tensile strength of the wall, the cup tears, usually near the punch radius where the wall is thinnest. A larger $D/d$ means a larger flange to draw in and a larger force, so at the LDR the force just reaches the wall strength. An estimate of the force for a quick check is $F\approx\pi d t\,\sigma_{UTS}\,(D/d-0.7)$, a commonly used approximation, where $\sigma_{UTS}$ is the ultimate tensile strength (MPa).

blocks.title: Estimating the drawing force
blocks.prompt: The 60 mm cup above is drawn from steel sheet of thickness $t=1.0$ mm and ultimate tensile strength 350 MPa (typical for deep-drawing quality steel). Estimate the maximum punch force.
blocks.answer: The punch force is about 80 kN, an order-of-magnitude figure used to size the press.

rows: Compressive hoop stress, blank holder force too low
Raise blank holder force; add draw beads
Near punch radius at the base
Draw force above wall strength: DR too high, holder force too high, too much friction, small radii
Lower draw ratio, lubricate die and flange, enlarge radii, add an anneal and redraw
Trim; use material with low planar anisotropy
blocks.caption: Common deep-drawing defects

blocks.markdown: The **blank holder** clamps the flange against the die face. It must be firm enough to suppress wrinkling (where the circumferential compression buckles the thin flange) but not so firm that friction under the holder raises the draw force until the wall tears. Lubrication of the die face, die radius and blank surface lowers friction, reduces the punch force and so allows a higher limiting drawing ratio; the punch surface, by contrast, is generally left dry or rough because friction between the cup wall and the punch helps carry the load into the wall.

blocks.title: The process window
blocks.text: There is a window of blank holder force: below it the flange wrinkles, above it the cup tears. Friction and lubrication move the window. Good lubrication on the die side and flange lowers the tearing force and widens the window.

blocks.title: Do not trust a single-draw ratio beyond the LDR
blocks.text: Draw ratios above about 2 need redrawing in stages, usually with reduced draws (typically smaller ratios per redraw) and intermediate annealing because work hardening lowers ductility. The values given here are typical, not guaranteed for your material.

points: Blank diameter for a flat-bottomed cup is $D=\sqrt{d^2+4dh}$ from equal surface areas, and the draw ratio is $D/d$.
The limiting drawing ratio is typically 1.8 to 2.0 for a single draw; beyond it the cup wall tears.
Wrinkling comes from flange compression with too little holding force; tearing comes from excessive draw force.
The blank holder force and lubrication together set the window between wrinkling and tearing.

questions.stem: A cup drawn from steel sheet shows buckled, wavy flange edges but no tears. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Blank holder force too high
Blank holder force too low
Draw ratio below the limit
Excessive punch lubrication

distractorRationale.a: Too much holder force would raise friction and tend to cause tearing near the punch radius, not flange buckling.
distractorRationale.c: A low draw ratio gives a small flange and less compressive stress, making wrinkling less likely.
distractorRationale.d: Lubricating the punch lowers friction on the punch, which raises tearing risk if anything; it does not produce flange buckling.

questions.explanation: Flange wrinkling is the buckling of the circumferentially compressed flange, which the blank holder is designed to suppress. Low holder force leaves the flange free to buckle.

questions.stem: A cylindrical cup has inside diameter 40 mm and height 30 mm. Ignoring corner radii and thinning, calculate the required blank diameter in mm.
questions.explanation: Equating cup surface area to blank area gives $D=\sqrt{d^2+4dh}=\sqrt{40^2+4(40)(30)}=\sqrt{1600+4800}=\sqrt{6400}=80$ mm. The draw ratio is then $80/40=2.0$, right at the typical limit.

questions.stem: What does the limiting drawing ratio (LDR) of a sheet metal represent?

options.text: The ratio of cup height to cup diameter
The ratio of final to initial sheet thickness
The ratio of punch force to blank holder force
The largest blank-to-punch diameter ratio that can be drawn in one operation without tearing

questions.correctOptionText: The largest blank-to-punch diameter ratio that can be drawn in one operation without tearing

distractorRationale.a: Cup height over diameter is a geometric depth measure, not the LDR.
distractorRationale.b: Thickness change is a separate effect; the LDR concerns diameters.
distractorRationale.c: A force ratio is not what limits the geometry directly; LDR is about diameters.

questions.explanation: The LDR is the maximum $D/d$ for a successful single draw, typically about 1.8 to 2.0. Beyond it the load needed to draw the flange exceeds the strength of the cup wall.

questions.stem: A steel sheet has a limiting drawing ratio of 1.9. What is the largest blank diameter, in mm, that can be drawn in a single operation into a cup of inside diameter 110 mm?
questions.explanation: The limit is $D_{max}=\text{LDR}\times d=1.9\times110=209$ mm. A larger blank would require a redraw or a smaller cup.

questions.stem: A cup tears cleanly around the base just above the punch radius. Which change is most likely to cure this without changing the material?

options.text: Lubricate the die face and flange and enlarge the die and punch radii
Increase the blank holder force
Use a bigger blank
Roughen the die face

questions.correctOptionText: Lubricate the die face and flange and enlarge the die and punch radii

distractorRationale.b: More holder force raises friction under the holder and increases the draw force, making tearing worse.
distractorRationale.c: A larger blank raises the draw ratio and so the force, making tearing more likely.
distractorRationale.d: Rougher die surfaces raise friction and the drawing force.

questions.explanation: Tearing occurs where the force transmitted through the wall exceeds its strength. Lower friction and larger radii reduce the draw force, so the wall can carry the load.

questions.stem: On a deep-drawing press, why is the die side lubricated but the punch side often left relatively dry?

options.text: Lubrication on the punch causes wrinkling
The die cannot work when dry
Friction at the punch helps carry load into the wall, while friction at the die and flange raises the force needed
Dry punches increase the draw ratio directly

questions.correctOptionText: Friction at the punch helps carry load into the wall, while friction at the die and flange raises the force needed

distractorRationale.a: Wrinkling is controlled by the holder force and flange stress, not punch lubrication.
distractorRationale.b: The die works but needs more force and risks tearing; this overstates the need.
distractorRationale.d: The draw ratio is a geometric ratio of diameters, and is not changed by punch friction.

questions.explanation: Friction on the die and flange opposes the inward flow of the flange and increases the load that the wall must carry. Friction on the punch face acts in the beneficial direction and relieves the wall near the punch corner.

questions.stem: A cup of inside diameter 50 mm and height 30 mm is drawn from steel sheet of thickness 0.8 mm with ultimate tensile strength 300 MPa. First find the blank diameter by area equality, then estimate the punch force in kN using $F\approx\pi d t\sigma_{UTS}(D/d-0.7)$.
A cup is drawn successfully at a draw ratio of 1.7. The tool is changed to give a blank holder force far above the correct range. What is the most probable result?

options.text: Heavy wrinkling in the flange
Improved formability and a higher LDR
No change, because holder force is irrelevant
Tearing at the punch radius

distractorRationale.a: Wrinkling is the symptom of too little holder force.
distractorRationale.b: Excess holder force reduces formability by raising friction and draw force.
distractorRationale.c: Holder force is a primary variable and changes the outcome.

questions.explanation: A very high holder force clamps the flange so tightly that friction rises sharply, increasing the draw force until the wall at the punch radius fractures. The correct force lies between the wrinkling and tearing limits.

questions.stem: Explain the role of the blank holder force in deep drawing. Describe what happens if it is too low and too high, and say why lubrication allows a wider range of acceptable holder force.
markingGuide: Holder clamps the flange against the die face
Too low: circumferential compression in the flange causes buckling and wrinkling
Too high: friction under the holder raises the draw force above wall strength, causing tearing
Lubrication lowers friction on the flange and die, reducing the draw force and the tearing risk
So the process window between wrinkling and tearing widens
questions.explanation: The holder keeps the flange flat; too little force lets it wrinkle and too much makes friction tear the wall. Lubrication lowers the friction contribution, widening the acceptable range.

questions.stem: A designer asks for a cylindrical steel cup of diameter 40 mm and depth 100 mm from sheet. Show using area equality why a single draw will fail, and describe the sequence of operations that could still make the part, including the role of intermediate annealing.
markingGuide: Draw ratio $\approx3.3$, far above the typical LDR of about 1.8 to 2.0
Hence a single draw would tear the wall at the punch radius
First draw to a larger diameter cup, then redraw (and perhaps re-redraw) through smaller dies with smaller ratios
Intermediate annealing restores ductility lost to work hardening; lubrication and generous radii help each stage
questions.explanation: The blank diameter is about 133 mm, a draw ratio of 3.3 which is beyond the single-draw limit. The cup must therefore be drawn in stages with redraws and occasional anneals.
